suggestions.reason: A day-by-day plan for the week so nothing gets left to the last minute

content.text: Interview Prep Plan
Goal: walk in knowing the company, the role, my best stories, and what I want to ask. Work through one block per day.
Days 1-2: Research
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Fill in the Company research brief
Look up each interviewer on LinkedIn and add them to the Interviewers table
Days 3-4: Stories and practice
Write 6-8 STAR stories in the Story bank
Answer every question in the Practice questions table out loud
Do one timed mock interview with a friend
Day 5-6: Polish
Finalize my 60-second pitch
Pick 5 questions to ask the interviewers
Test video call setup, or plan the route and arrival time
Day before and day of
Lay out outfit, print resume copies, charge devices
Skim the research brief and story headlines one last time
Send thank-you emails within 24 hours after

suggestions.title: Company research brief
suggestions.reason: One place to capture what the company does, how it makes money, and where it's headed

content.text: Company Research Brief
What they do
One-sentence summary of the product, who the customers are (consumers, SMBs, banks, enterprises), and the problem it solves.
Business model
Revenue sources: interchange, subscription, interest/lending spread, SaaS fees, payments volume?
Funding stage, latest round, key investors
Key growth metrics I can find (users, TPV, AUM, ARR)
Competitors and positioning
Top 3 competitors and how this company differs
Their moat: tech, distribution, licenses, data?
Regulation and risk
Which licenses or regulators matter (bank partner, money transmitter, SEC, CFPB)? Note how compliance, fraud and security show up in the role.
Recent news
Read the last 3 press releases or blog posts
Check recent news for launches, layoffs, funding or regulatory issues
Why me, why them
Draft 3 sentences linking my experience to their mission and the role's top needs.

content.text: Notice & message templates
Copy, edit, and send. Check your local landlord-tenant law for required notice periods and wording before sending formal notices.
Rent reminder
Hi [Name], a friendly reminder that rent of $[amount] for [month] is due on the 1st. Let me know if you have any questions. Thank you!
Late rent notice
Hi [Name], I haven't received rent of $[amount] for [month], which was due on [date]. A late fee of $[fee] applies per the lease. Please pay by [date] or contact me to discuss.
Notice of entry
Hi [Name], I'll need to enter the unit on [date] between [time window] to [reason: repair / inspection / showing]. Please let me know if that time is a problem.
Lease renewal offer
Hi [Name], your lease ends on [date]. I'd like to offer a [12]-month renewal at $[new rent]/month. Please let me know by [date] if you'd like to renew.

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

Our team wiki has grown organically over several years and now lives in a tool that few people enjoy using. Pages are hard to find, ownership is unclear, and a good share of the content is out of date. This project moves the wiki into PlexiiWrite and uses the move as a chance to clean house, so that we end up with a smaller, more trustworthy knowledge base rather than a copy of the old one in a new place.
Goals
The migration should deliver a wiki that people actually reach for first when they have a question. To judge whether we have succeeded, we will look at four outcomes:
All active, useful content is available in PlexiiWrite, organized under a structure the team has agreed on.
Every retained page has a named owner and a last-reviewed date.
Search returns the right page for common questions within the first few results.
The old wiki is set to read-only and then retired, so there is a single source of truth.
Scope

In scope is the full content inventory of the current wiki, including pages, attachments, and embedded images. We will audit this content, archive or delete what is obsolete, restructure what remains, and import it into PlexiiWrite. The project also covers setting up workspace permissions, creating a few page templates for recurring document types, and running a short onboarding session for the team.

Out of scope are rewriting pages that are accurate but merely imperfect, integrating PlexiiWrite with other tools beyond basic single sign-on, and migrating content that belongs to other departments' wikis. If a request falls outside these lines, it goes on a follow-up list rather than expanding this project.
Timeline
The work is planned across six weeks, with some flexibility built in for review cycles.
Week 1: Inventory every page, tag each as keep, update, or archive, and agree on the new top-level structure.
Week 2: Configure the PlexiiWrite workspace, permissions, and templates, and run a small test import to check formatting and attachments.
Weeks 3 and 4: Import approved content in batches, with page owners fixing formatting problems and broken links as they go.
Week 5: Run a team-wide review, hold the onboarding session, and collect feedback on structure and search.
Week 6: Freeze the old wiki, make final corrections, announce the cutover, and set a date for retirement.
Roles

One project lead will own the schedule and decisions. Each major section of the wiki has a content owner responsible for deciding what stays and verifying it after import. An administrator handles workspace setup, permissions, and the technical side of the import.
Risks

The largest risk is content owners not finding time for the audit, which would stall the import. We will reduce this by assigning small, clearly bounded sections and setting a firm deadline for keep or archive decisions at the end of week 1.

Formatting loss during import is likely for complex tables, embedded files, and internal links. The test import in week 2 is meant to surface these early so we can decide whether to fix them in bulk or by hand.

Adoption is a quieter risk. If people keep editing the old wiki after cutover, content will fragment again. Making the old wiki read-only on a communicated date, and pointing its home page to PlexiiWrite, addresses this directly.

Finally, a restructure can feel disruptive even when it is an improvement. Involving the team in naming the top-level categories and keeping the first-week structure simple should help people feel the new layout is theirs.
Next Steps
Confirm the project lead and section owners, schedule the week 1 inventory kickoff, and request PlexiiWrite workspace access for the administrator.

content.text: Welcome to the team

You are joining the team that customers talk to when something is confusing, broken, or important to them. This guide covers what your first week looks like, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations. Read it through once before your first day, then keep it open as a reference. Nobody expects you to remember everything. We expect you to ask questions early and often.

Our approach to support comes down to three ideas. Solve the customer's actual problem, not just the question they typed. Be honest about what we know and what we don't. And when a problem is beyond you, hand it off cleanly rather than letting it sit.
Your first week
The first week is designed to build confidence gradually. You will watch, then assist, then handle tickets yourself with a safety net.

On day one, you will get access to your accounts, meet your onboarding buddy, and spend time with your team lead going over expectations and schedule. Spend the rest of the day setting up your tools and reading through our knowledge base, starting with the most-viewed articles. These cover the questions customers ask most.

On day two, you will shadow an experienced agent for several hours, listening to how they phrase answers, how they research, and when they escalate. Take notes on anything that surprises you. In the afternoon, read through twenty or so recently solved tickets, including a few that were rated poorly, so you can see the difference.
On day three, you will start drafting replies to live tickets. Your buddy reviews each draft before it goes out. This feels slow, but it is the fastest way to learn our voice and product details.
On day four, you will send replies on lower-complexity tickets without pre-review, while your buddy spot-checks them afterward. You will also sit in on a team standup and a quality review session.

On day five, you will handle a normal mix of tickets with light oversight. Finish the week with a short one-on-one with your team lead to talk about what went well, what felt hard, and what to focus on in week two.
The tools you will use
You will spend most of your day in a handful of systems. Learn these well and the rest gets easier.
The help desk is where every customer conversation lives, whether it arrives by email, chat, or web form. You will assign, tag, reply to, and close tickets here.
The knowledge base holds our public help articles and internal troubleshooting notes. Search it before answering anything, and link customers to articles when it helps.
Team chat is for quick questions, handoffs, and incident announcements. Use the support channel for general questions and the incidents channel for outages.
The admin console lets you view customer accounts, plans, and recent activity. Treat it as read-mostly. Only make changes you have been trained on, and note every change in the ticket.
The issue tracker is where engineering manages bugs. You will search it to see whether a problem is already known and file new reports when it is not.
The status page shows current system health. Check it at the start of every shift and before answering any report that sounds like an outage.
Your team lead will walk you through access and permissions. If something does not work on day one, tell us right away so it does not slow you down later.
How we write to customers

Good support replies are clear, warm, and complete. Start by acknowledging what the customer is trying to do, then give the answer or next step in plain language. Avoid jargon unless the customer used it first. If you need information from them, ask for everything you need in one message rather than trickling out questions.

Never guess. If you are not sure, say you are checking and give a realistic time for your next update. Never promise a fix date that engineering has not confirmed. Apologize when we are at fault, briefly and sincerely, and then move on to what happens next.
Before sending, reread the customer's original message and make sure you answered every question in it. Most poor ratings come from a reply that was polite but missed something.
How we handle escalations

An escalation is a handoff to someone with more access, expertise, or authority. It is a normal part of the job, and escalating at the right time is a sign of good judgment. The mistake is waiting too long or escalating without enough detail.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of the following is true:
The issue looks like a bug or outage affecting more than one customer.
The customer reports data loss, a security concern, or an unauthorized charge.
The fix requires access or permissions you do not have.
The customer is requesting a refund, exception, or credit beyond your approval limit.
You have worked on the ticket for around thirty minutes without a clear path forward.
The customer has asked for a manager, or the conversation is becoming hostile.
Severity levels

We use three levels to decide how fast something moves. Critical issues are outages, security incidents, or data loss, and they go to the on-call engineer and your team lead immediately through the incidents channel. High issues block a customer from doing core work but have no known wide impact, and they should be escalated to the second-tier team within the hour. Normal issues are everything else that needs specialist input, and they go to the second-tier queue with a standard handoff.
Writing a good handoff

Whoever picks up your escalation should not need to ask the customer anything again. Before you hand off, write an internal note that includes a one-sentence summary of the problem, the customer's account and plan, exact steps to reproduce if applicable, what you have already tried, relevant screenshots or logs, and the severity you believe it deserves. Then tag the ticket correctly and post a link in the right channel if the severity calls for it.
Staying involved

Escalating does not mean the customer becomes someone else's problem. Tell the customer what is happening, who is looking at it, and when they can expect an update. Remain the point of contact unless the receiving team takes over directly. Check in on the ticket at the time you promised, even if the answer is that there is no news yet. When the issue is resolved, confirm with the customer and add a note on the cause so the team can learn from it.
Who to ask for help

Your onboarding buddy is your first stop for day-to-day questions. Your team lead handles scheduling, performance, and anything you are uncomfortable raising elsewhere. For product or technical questions, use the support channel, where experienced agents will usually respond quickly. For urgent issues, follow the severity process above rather than waiting for a reply.
There are no embarrassing questions in your first month. A thirty-second question to a teammate is always cheaper than a wrong answer to a customer.
What success looks like at 30 days

By the end of your first month, we hope you can handle most standard tickets on your own, find answers in the knowledge base quickly, write clean escalation notes, and recognize the difference between a normal issue and an urgent one. Your team lead will review your progress with you at the 30-day mark and agree on goals for the next quarter.
First-week checklist
Accounts and permissions confirmed for every tool
Introduction meeting with your onboarding buddy and team lead
Top knowledge base articles read
Shadowing session completed
At least ten reviewed draft replies
Escalation process reviewed with your buddy
End-of-week one-on-one scheduled
Welcome aboard. We are glad you are here.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. In the next few minutes we will cover what makes a bug report useful, so that the person who picks it up can fix it quickly instead of chasing you for details.

slides.title: Why report quality matters
bullets: A vague report costs hours of back and forth
Developers can only fix what they can see
Clear reports get triaged and fixed sooner
Good reports build trust between teams
Duplicates and lost tickets drop sharply
slides.notes: Think of a bug report as a handoff. If the reader has to guess, the fix slows down or the ticket gets ignored. A few extra minutes from you can save the team hours.

slides.title: Start with a precise title and summary
bullets: Name the problem, not the feeling
Say what broke and where
Weak: "Checkout is broken"
Strong: "Checkout button does nothing after applying a promo code"
Add one sentence on the impact
slides.notes: The title is what people see in lists and search results, so make it specific enough that someone can recognize the bug without opening it. Follow it with a short summary of who is affected and how badly.

slides.title: Give steps to reproduce
bullets: Number each step in the order you took it
Include the exact data, account or input you used
State the expected result
State the actual result
Note how often it happens: always, sometimes, once
slides.notes: This is the most valuable part of the report. If a developer can follow your steps and see the bug within a minute, you have done your job. Always separate what you expected from what actually happened.

slides.title: Add the evidence and context
bullets: Screenshots or a short screen recording
Error messages copied word for word
Browser, device, OS and app version
Environment: production, staging or local
Logs or console output if you can get them
slides.notes: Evidence turns a claim into something checkable. Attach it directly to the ticket rather than describing it, and always include the version and environment, since bugs often depend on them.

slides.title: Before you hit submit
bullets: Search for an existing report first
Report one problem per ticket
Reread your steps as if you were a stranger
Set a sensible severity and be honest about it
Stay available to answer follow-up questions
slides.notes: Run this quick checklist every time. The best test is to imagine a teammate who knows nothing about your situation and ask whether they could act on the ticket. If yes, send it.

Subject: Kickoff for the Plexii Pulse launch

Hi team,

Thanks for making time this week. Plexii Pulse is our next major launch, and this note covers what we are aiming for, how the next eight weeks are laid out, and who owns each piece. Please read it before our kickoff call so we can spend the meeting on questions rather than recap.

What we are trying to achieve

  • Ship Plexii Pulse to all customers on the planned launch date, with no critical issues open at go-live.
  • Give customers a clear reason to try it, supported by a launch page, in-app announcement, and updated help content on day one.
  • Have support and sales ready to answer questions confidently before anything goes public.
  • Set up tracking from the start so we can report on adoption within the first 30 days.

Timeline

Weeks Phase What should be done by the end
1 to 2 Scope and plan Final scope agreed, success metrics set, messaging brief drafted
3 to 5 Build Feature complete, analytics in place, launch assets in first draft
6 Internal and beta testing Bugs triaged, beta feedback reviewed, support and sales briefed

Who owns what

Overall project Product lead Scope, schedule, decisions, and the go or no-go call
Build and release Engineering lead Development, quality, rollout plan, and performance

How we will work

We will hold a 30-minute check-in every Tuesday and Thursday, and each owner should bring a short status in green, yellow, or red. Day-to-day questions go in the project channel so everyone sees the same information. If something puts a date at risk, raise it right away rather than waiting for the next check-in. Purpose

This meeting confirms whether we are ready to launch on the planned date. By the end, we will have a clear go or no-go decision, a list of open risks with named owners, and agreed next steps for the final days before launch.

Product, Engineering, QA, Design, Marketing, Customer Support, Operations, and the executive sponsor. Each function should arrive ready to state its readiness status in one or two sentences.

results.text:
Refund Policy FAQ

Can I get a refund?

Yes. If you are not happy with your purchase, you can request a full refund within 30 days of the date you were charged. No explanation is needed.

What happens after 30 days?

Once the 30-day window has passed, we do not offer refunds on monthly plans or other one-time purchases. You can still cancel at any time to stop future charges, and you will keep access until the end of the period you have already paid for.

Do annual plans work differently?

They do. Annual plans are refunded pro rata, which means you get back the value of the time you have not used. If you cancel within the first 30 days, you receive a full refund. After that, we refund the remaining unused portion of your annual term.

How is a pro rata refund calculated?

We divide the price you paid by the length of the term and refund the unused share. For example, if you paid $120 for a year and cancel after three months, you have used one quarter of the plan, so you would receive $90 back.

How do I request a refund?

Contact our support team from your account and tell us which plan you would like refunded. We will confirm the amount before processing it, and the money returns to your original payment method.

Will I lose access when I am refunded?

Yes. A refund ends your paid access to the plan, effective when the refund is processed. If you only want to stop renewal and keep using the service until your term ends, cancel your plan instead of requesting a refund.
